scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition dates back to at least the 1400s in coastal Mozambique, where Chopi ancestors experimented with wooden percussion.
The specific choreographic motifs—including the use of shields and spears—were heavily influenced by 19th-century conflicts with the Zulu people.
The Mozambican Civil War (1975–1992) significantly disrupted the practice, leading to its current status as an endangered heritage.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Timbila is performed at weddings and community gatherings to chronicle local history and social issues.
The m’zeno song within the dance serves as a humorous and sarcastic critique of contemporary life.
It is a primary marker of Chopi identity and cultural independence.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform in groups of two to twelve in a line or formation in front of the xylophone orchestra.
The movement style is described as 'warrior-like,' featuring rhythmic steps that synchronize with the complex polyrhythms of the timbila.
Dancers often carry shields and spears, using them to punctuate the rhythm.
Watch for Warrior Step, M'zeno Song Accompaniment.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear or small group formation (2-12 people) positioned in front of the seated orchestra.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is produced by an orchestra of 5 to 30 timbila xylophones.
These are made from mwenje wood with calabash resonators.
Listen for the Chilanzane (xylophone), Debiinda (xylophone), Chikhulu (xylophone), Calabash resonators.
The pulse is Complex/Polyrhythmic.

A rich, buzzing nasal sound produced by wooden slats over calabash resonators. The music is characterized by dense polyrhythms where the orchestra creates a wall of sound with varying pitches and registers.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear costumes inspired by Zulu military dress, which may include animal skins or fibers.
Key props include shields, spears, and wooden clubs (head-breakers).
Performances typically take place in open community spaces during weddings or social events, with the orchestra seated and the dancers positioned prominently in front.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The tradition is maintained by 'timbila masters' (mestres musicais), who are responsible for both the complex craftsmanship of the instruments and the composition of new musical works each year.

While centered in the Zavala district of Inhambane, the term 'mbila' or 'timbila' is used across Southern Africa to refer to various xylophones and lamellophones, such as the Venda 'mbila dza madeza' in South Africa.
The tradition is traditionally passed from father to son through apprenticeship.
